title: Engendering Chinese Cultures
requirements:
UGED3205 is double-coded with GDRS3012. Not for Gender Studies Majors; and students who have taken GDRS2007, 3012 or UGED2205. 
Co-requisite: Any course with “UGFH” or “UGFN” as prefix
description: (UGED3205 is double-coded with GDRS3012.) The Chinese Century witnesses increasing local, regional, and global interests on China. In this spectacular era, Chinese culture has become a mediation of China’s economic activities, political institutions, social dynamics, and ordinary life patterns. Gender, as a major building block of society and culture, provides us with an analytical lens to understand how diverse forms of Chinese culture anchor feelings, thoughts, and actions invested within and beyond China.Covering academic research, historical materials, and contemporary cultural productions, this course introduces to students selected issues including history and modernity from late Ming dynasty to the New China, popular culture in contemporary era, the cultural productions of sexual minorities, and, finally, the regional debates over gendered diaspora and Chineseness. As they participate in learning activities of the course, students will be gradually led to understanding Chinese culture from a new perspective. Furthermore, students will have a chance to reflect on long-held values and beliefs which they have acquired as members of this culture, or which they witness in the daily life of the community around them. While unpacking the complexity and nuances of Chinese culture from a gender perspective, this course resonates with the Sustainable Development Goals (SDG) adopted by United Nations, including SDG 5 (Gender Equality), SDG 10 (Reduced Inequalities). Students reflect on their various values and concepts in daily life through this course, and become a global citizen with an open mind.

title: Women's Narratives and Hong Kong History
requirements:
UGED3206 is double-coded with GDRS3011. 
Not for Gender Studies Majors and students who have taken GDRS2008, 3011 or UGED2206.
Co-requisite: Any course with “UGFH” or “UGFN” as prefix
description: (UGED3206 is double-coded with GDRS3011.)  This course will revisit Hong Kong’s history through the exploration of narratives documenting women, a group often made invisible in history writing, as social actors in the fabric of colonial and post-colonial Hong Kong. From elites’ households to squatter huts, from brothels, textile factories to convents and schools, from public housing estates, prison, government offices to LegCo Chamber, women of different generations and ethnicities have been active players, caregivers, breadwinners, and pioneers, contesting the prescribed gender role and identity in a patriarchal society. The course seeks to not only explore how they lived, or how their lives are shaped and reshaped by their own unyielding efforts but also the different times they inhabited, but also to see how their stories can find ways into narratives and representations, both fictional, historical, and autobiographical. Drawing from a wide range of historical, fictional, and documentary sources, images and oral histories, this course will introduce a multi-faceted history of Hong Kong with women as the focus of inquiry. Through lectures, interactive tutorials, group projects and self-study, students will learn to relate the personal to social, political and economic changes in Hong Kong. Through critical exercise and personal reflection on Hong Kong history and the role of women in it, the course engages directly with the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) adopted by all United Nations Member States in 2015 by engaging directly with the SDGs 5 (Gender Equality), 10 (Reduced Inequalities) and 16 (Peace, Justice, and Strong Institutions).

title: Love and Intimate Relationship
requirements:
UGED3208 is double-coded with GDRS3004. 
Not for Gender Studies Majors; and students who have taken GDRS3004. 
Co-requisite: Any course with “UGFH” or “UGFN” as prefix
description: (UGED3208 is double-coded with GDRS3004.)  This course reviews basic concepts, theories and research findings of romantic love and intimate relationship. Various aspects of romantic love and intimate relationship will be critically reviewed. Based on research from a wide range of disciplines including gender studies, cultural studies, sociology, psychology, counselling, media studies, among various fields, together with input from literature and popular culture, the course will cover major areas such as the following: how do we understand the notions of “love” and “intimacy” in the different social and personal contexts, what are the different stages in a relationship; the influence of cultural myths and social scripts; interpersonal processes within romantic relationships (such as attraction, social cognition, communication and conflicts, etc.); how social gender role shapes romantic feelings and behaviors; notions of equality and freedom within relationships; power and violence; intimate relationship across life span, etc. Students are encouraged to actively reflect upon their own life experience, to engage in critical discussions of cultural phenomenon through case studies, and learn to untangle the cultural myths, norms, and stereotypes that shapes our private lives and our society in general. Upon the completion of the course, students should demonstrate basic understanding of structure, functions, dynamics, and development of romantic love and other interpersonal relationship. The personal is political. As personal relationships are the most basic social relationships that makes up the larger network of social relationships, it is hope that students could use knowledge from this course as an insight to understand, develop, and improve the quality of their own interpersonal relationship, and would aspire to build a more open and equal society starting from equalitarian and mindful personal relationships. Through critical exercise and personal reflection on notions and experience of Love and Intimate Relationship in relations to notions such as power, diversity, equality, and freedom, the course engages directly with the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) adopted by all United Nations Member States in 2015 by engaging directly with the SDGs 5 (Gender Equality), 10 (Reduced Inequalities) and 16 (Peace, Justice, and Strong Institution).
outcome: Expected Learning Goals  1.       Understand the knowledge base of romantic love and intimate relationship  2.       Be equipped with the research methods in romantic love and intimate relationship from multiple disciplines such as psychology, cultural studies, sociology, philosophy and anthropology  3.       Relate the knowledge on love and intimate relationships that they learn from the course to their everyday life  4.       Develop their own values on love and intimate relationships after considering relevant theoretical views and empirical research  5.       Gain insights about romantic love and intimate relationship  6.    Critically reflect on gender and other inequalities in society and interpersonal relationships   Learning Outcomes  ·         Understand, relate and apply the key romantic love and intimate relationship concepts to daily life  ·         Critically engage with gender and other inequalities in society and interpersonal relationships  ·         Familiarize with the key classical and contemporary research findings in romantic love and intimate relationship  ·         Conceptualize, structure, articulate and present original ideas, both in written assignments and during tutorial discussions, on romantic love and intimate relationship related topics  ·         Design, direct and regulate own study plan for problem-based learning, from identifying the problem, setting learning objectives, researching on relevant information, reflecting on what has been learnt, to applying the knowledge to future problems

title: Buddhism and Contemporary Life
requirements:
UGED3322 is double-coded with CURE3145.Not for Cultural Studies; Public Humanities; Religious Studies; Theology Majors; and students who have taken CURE3145 or UGED2331.
Co-requisite: Any course with “UGFH” or “UGFN” as prefix
description: (UGED3322 is double-coded with CURE3145.)   This course studies Buddhism and contemporary life in the context of the new development of Buddhism. It examines how Buddhism is reinvented and reconceptualized to make it meaningful for men and women living in modern complex society of the information age. Based on the recent development of Buddhism in both Asia and in the West, this course discusses how Buddhism responds to contemporary issues facing contemporary men and women. Topics include the Buddhist approach to economic development and human right, pollution and biotechnology, feminism, Buddhist ethics and the issues of abortion, euthanasia and suicide, Buddhism and interfaith dialogue.
outcome: u        To encourage students to probe deeper into the ground of existence and develop a wider context of meaning of life through a critical study of the development of Buddhism in modern society.u        To help student understand how religion can exert positive influences on human life and modern society through the case of Buddhism

title: Science and Religion
requirements:
UGED3430 is double-coded with CURE3375. Not for Cultural Studies; Public Humanities; Religious Studies; Theology Majors; and students who have taken CURE3375. 
Co-requisite: Any course with “UGFH” or “UGFN” as prefix
description: (UGED3430 is double-coded with CURE3375.)  This course mainly investigates the relationship between religion and natural sciences. The course will cover the following aspects: 1) historical investigation of the relationship between religion and natural sciences; 2) comparison between methodology of natural sciences and religious studies; and 3) religious dealings with different issues arising from scientific discoveries and technological advancements; ecology and religion; and the nature of science and religion in the postmodern culture.

title: Beethoven in China and the West
requirements:
Not for Music Majors. 
Co-requisite: UGFH1000 or UGFN1000 (only applicable to students admitted to the 4-year curriculum)
description: In the West, Beethoven is widely regarded as the greatest composer in the history of music and even of mankind. The stories of Beethoven’s broken family, failed love-life, and hearing loss have enthralled Western audiences as much as the sounds of his piano sonatas, string quartets, and symphonies. When the Berlin Wall was demolished in 1989, it was accompanied by Beethoven’s “Ode to Joy.” Yet, despite Western claims to Beethoven’s universality, nowhere else in the non-Western world is Beethoven held in such esteem–except for China. Since the late (if not even early) twentieth century, Beethoven has had more admirers in China than in the West. Who exactly is this Beethoven? And how was it that he, an Austro-German composer who read into Hinduism but never (so far is as currently known) into Confucianism, became a cultural icon both for and of the Chinese? Scholars still just do not know. In this course, we will try to figure it out for ourselves. By listening to and viewing Beethoven’s masterworks and hearing/seeing them in both their original Western and Chinese contexts, we will debate what makes this one person collectively Western, Chinese, and universal (or not). In addition to listening and reading assignments, students will research an independent essay/concert review on Beethoven and his music, whether in Greater China, the West, or both. The abilities to read or hear music are not required to excel in this class.

title: Body , Mind and Spirituality: Classics of India
requirements:
Not for Philosophy Majors.
Co-requisite: UGFH1000, UGFN1000 or UGFN1001 (only applicable to students admitted to the 4-year curriculum)
description: India, with its rich and colorful culture in spirituality, has produced numerous classics on the subject throughout history, which have influenced the region and the rest of the world for centuries. This course is designed to guide students to read and to have dialogue with some Indian classics in religion, philosophy, and health science, including Ṛgveda, Upaniṣads, Bhagavad Gītā, Āyurveda, Yoga-sūtra, and etc., through which they are expected to learn the unique contributions of Indian culture to the subjects of body, mind, and spirituality.

title: Chinese Material Culture
requirements:
UGED2285 is double-coded with CUMT2004. 
Not for Cultural Management (CUMS and CUMT) Majors; and students who have taken CUMT2004.
Co-requisite: Any course with “UGFH” or “UGFN” as prefix
description: (UGED2285 is double-coded with CUMT2004.) This is a cross-disciplinary course straddles the studies of history, anthropology, and sociology from the perspective of material objects. The course intends to achieve two goals: first, it leads students to identify and appreciate the traditional Chinese values, which include the teachings of Confucianism and Daoism, embodied in the many production types pertinent to what we now regard as Chinese; and second, it explains how those various material types ended up being included and translated as the representative categories of Chinese civilization throughout the historical times. The course will begin from the basic by introducing the mainstream material productions from ancient to modern China: jades, antique bronzes, lacquer, ceramics, architecture, silk, as well as grave goods. The discussions instruct students to appreciate these essential elements of Chinese culture from the perspectives of their physical qualities, craftsmanship, and historical values. They are also to encourage students to think about the roles of material objects in shaping cultural, ethnic, and even national identities.
outcome: Upon completion of the course, students would be able to identify the material and artistic features of some mainstream Chinese artifacts; develop interests in Chinese culture from the perspective of objects; identify key historical sites and remains of pre-modern China; develop acute senses for appreciating traditions and values; develop interests in culture and history; analyze the sources of Chinese heritage and traditions; think critically about historical and other relevant cultural presentations; and get prepared for further trainings in the disciplines of art history, archaeology, anthropology and history.
syllabus: 1. Introduction: What is the present view about Chinese material culture?  Present-day China received huge inheritance from the many groups of people and cultural traditions that existed in antiquity. This session introduce a range of material culture that makes up the broad family of Chinese culture. The most important types include jades, antique bronzes, lacquer, ceramics, and architecture. The definitions given here hope to broaden the scope and include the less-discussed categories of clothing and costumes, sculpture, and grave goods. This overview leads students to consider the many sources of traditional values now embodied in the material culture that we now describe as ‘Chinese’.  2. Jades In China, jades have always been understood to have spiritual power and artistic values. What is the scientific definition of jades? How did Confucius and his contemporaries define the roles of jades? How did their teachings shape the understanding of jades in Chinese society? And what are the present views about jades? This session will respond to this question by giving a review of jade history, usage and craftsmanship.  3. Antique bronzes Among the many treasures inherited from the past, bronzes are core collections that they are always found as representatives of ancient China in modern museums both in China and overseas. This session will describe different categories of bronzes and the motifs found on them in relation to their dates. It will also introduce the imperial collections found in the Kaogu tu, and later on in Xiqing gujian; and explain the values and significance of bronze collections in modern museums.   4. Lacquer Lacquer is a unique production of ancient China. This session introduces the complicated steps involved in its production, and reviews lacquer-using history in China and in other parts of Asia. The discussion leads student to become aware of the broad transmission of the lacquer-using traditions in Asia that shaped a central role for China in antiquity.  5. Sculpture In China, sculptural representation is closely tied with religious practices. This session will introduce the Buddhist sites in Henan and Sichuan, as well as the pictorial representations found in the Daoist temples in Hebei. The session will describe the renewed definition of sculpture in the modern times when the Western artistic values were received.  6. Architecture Architecture forms an essential part of material culture. In China, however, the studies of historical architecture began rather late. This session introduces the classic writings by Liang Sicheng, as well as the renowned Yingcao fasi, the Building Manual composed in the Song period, which founded the standardized Chinese construction works.   7. Silk Silk production began in the late Neolithic period. This session introduces the traditional steps in silk-making and weaving as found in craftsman handbooks published in the Ming period; and discusses how silk as commodity embodies the rich history of cultural exchange between China and the West through trade.  8. Ceramics Ceramics are representative productions of south China. This session introduces the production of the classic kilns of Ge, Yu, Ding, Longquan, and Jingdezhen. This session instructs students to identify the colour, texture, decoration, as well as motifs found on the ceramics produced in different areas. They embody rich aesthetic values deemed appropriate in Confucian classics.  9. Ornaments Chinese ornaments comprise an extended family of motifs that include flowers, birds, figures, beasts, characters, as well as scenes. This session discuss two key groups: plants and dragons. The former was adopted from both nature and religious practices; whereas the latter was acquired through cultural construction over time. This session discusses how the two genres merged along difference courses into what we understand as being Chinese today.   10. Chinese calligraphy and paintings Chinese calligraphy and paintings represent a major aesthetic system that includes the use of ink and brush, writing, as well as imagination particularly defined in Daoist writings. This session introduces the basic concepts of calligraphy and the features found in the classic paintings from the Song to the Qing periods.   11. Grave goods: objects for the deceased  Mingqi is a unique category of items produced in China. It is a group of goods created especially for the burial with the deceased that they are closely connected with the Chinese ideas about ghosts, spirits, and afterlife. This session will review the history of mingqi from as early as the Bronze Age, and look into how this understanding is translated in modern practice.  12. Antique collection and modern consumerism The antiquities of China provide a resourceful base for modern designers and cultural industries. In light of modern consuming practices, Chinese designers, architects, museum workers, historians, and other culture-related professionals fall back on inheritance to seek for ideas to create something new and unique for the country. This session reviews the concerns of relevant practitioners.   13. Conclusion  The concluding session outline the present ideas about material culture and its role in modern society, which is a topic that has become increasingly important in the spheres of anthropology and sociology. This session will combine the discussions on Chinese material culture and the discourse of object studies. This will give students ideas to develop interests in the study of China; and enable them to engage the past with the present.

title: Music and Meaning
requirements:
Not for Music Majors. 
Co-requisite: Any course with “UGFH” or “UGFN” as prefix
description: Why and how do people attach meaning to music? How is musical meaning related to other facets of human experience, such as action, emotion, thought and values? Is music really a ‘universal language’? How do we use music as a means of personal expression in various everyday situations, such as birthday celebrations, religious services, and school assemblies? How does music interact with other media, such as words and visual images, to communicate meaning? Can meaning exist in the internal structural relations of musical works without words or explicit extra-musical reference? This course explores these and other semiotic questions surrounding music through the examination of listening and music-making practices in diverse socio-cultural and aesthetic contexts, and includes examples drawn from Western classical, Chinese traditional, and various popular genres. Students will have the opportunity to apply the analytical methodologies introduced in this course towards critical reflections on musical experiences that they find personally meaningful.

title: Xiayi Spirit and Literature – From Tang Legends to Wuxia Novels
requirements:
Not for Chinese Language and Literature; and Chinese Language Studies and Chinese Language Education (CLED) Majors.
Co-requisite: Any course with “UGFH” or “UGFN” as prefix
description: A significant element in traditional Chinese culture, xiayi (chivalrous) spirit had been widely and highly deemed as a force of justice among the common people in particular the grass roots through generations, though it might be considered as trivia or heresy when compared to the dominant Confucian thoughts. Legends in the Tang dynasty, gongan stories in Song and Ming, xiayi novels in Qing, and the contemporary wuxia novels are all literary manifestations of this spirit. This course attempts to explore the spiritual profile of Chinese people and to analyse the characteristics of Chinese culture through the appreciation of this unique Chinese novel genre. Students will also be guided to learn more about traditional Chinese culture and the development of Chinese literature.

title: Ethnic Literature in China
requirements:
Not for Translation Majors.
Co-requisite: Any course with “UGFH” or “UGFN” as prefix
description: This course will explore the diversity of China’s literary heritage, with a focus on the generally “unsung” literatures of more peripheral groups: love poetry of the Himalayan foothills and ancient epics of Tibetan kings, to creation myths and contemporary stories about “being ethnic” in modern China. While the rise of China on the world stage has resulted in great interest in Chinese language and culture, this interest has been primarily focused on Han culture and standard forms of the Chinese language. Officially, China is comprised of 55 different ethnic minority peoples, alongside the Han majority. Each of these ethnicities has its own rich literary tradition, from folk tales to stories written in native scripts and modern compositions in Chinese.The course will feature video presentations of China’s more remote locales, as we get to grips with how literature reflects local identities. For ease of accessibility, readings will focus on works available in English translation, but students will also have the chance to learn some simple words and phrases from some of China’s lesser-known languages.

title: Personal Health and Fitness Programme Design
requirements:
UGED2620 is double-coded with SPED2301. 
Not for ESHE; SPED; PESH Majors; and students who have taken SPED2301. 
Co-requisite: Any course with “UGFH” or “UGFN” as prefix
description: (UGED2620 is double-coded with SPED2301.)  This course is designed to introduce basic knowledge in the relationship between exercise and personal health, and to encourage the adoption of healthy lifestyle habits. Practical knowledge including principles in developing and evaluation of a health based exercise programme will be the focus. Health related topics such as weight management, nutrition, muscular function, etc., will be discussed. Class format will be mainly mini-lectures, active exercise participation, group tutorials and discussion. Students will be required to develop personal muscular training program and aerobic exercise training program. This course will also enable students to pursue a "Personal Health and Fitness Proficiency Certificate".

title: Utopia and Dystopia
requirements:
Not for Philosophy Majors.
Co-requisite: UGFH1000, UGFN1000 or UGFN1001 (only applicable to students admitted to the 4-year curriculum)
description: The course provides students with a good understanding of the multifaceted relationships between Utopia and Dystopia. What does Utopia and Dystopia help us see about human nature, law and justice? Is the construction of Ideal World and Perfect Society possible? How can utopian thoughts or utopian experiments help us address contemporary social challenges? Why is it that utopian dream will always develop into dystopian nightmare? What warnings are provided by dystopian literature and film? Focus will be placed on philosophical reflections on the utopian and dystopian thoughts in the Chinese and Western culture.

title: (Re) Claiming the City
requirements:
UGED2922 is double-coded with URSP2020. 
Not for Urban Studies Majors; and students who have taken URSP2020. 
Co-requisite: Any course with “UGFH” or “UGFN” as prefix
description: (UGED2922 is double-coded with URSP2020.) Increasingly uneven and intensified processes of urbanization simultaneously generate serious challenges and exciting opportunities for urban populations across the globe. Contemporary cities are as much spaces of resonance, innovation, and emancipation as sites of violence, pollution, and alienation. This course revolves around the distinctive rhythms, experiences, and dynamics of urban life. What gives urban living its distinct characteristics? What current social, economic, and political problems deserve the attention of urban inhabitants? Which issues generate the greatest discord and motivate full coordination among different actors involved in governing cities? As urban life is characterized by both cosmopolitan conviviality and immense inequality, in this course students will learn about different modes of coexistence and exclusion in contemporary cities. Globalizing forms of urban protest arising from struggles over urban resources, space, and decision-making mechanisms will be investigated. By highlighting the complex and contested dynamics of urban life, the course will help students situate and interpret their everyday urban experiences at the intersection of multiple and interconnected flows, networks, and scales that are produced by the city and that produce it.

title: The Beauty of Kunqu Opera
requirements:
UGED1061 is double-coded with ARTS1001. Not for CHLL and CLED Majors; and students who have taken ARTS1001.
Co-requisite: Any course with “UGFH” or “UGFN” as prefix
description: (UGED1061 is double-coded with ARTS1001.)This course introduces students to the music, performance, literature and aesthetics of Kunqu opera in order to enhance their understanding of traditional Chinese culture, classical Chinese literature as well as performing arts. Selected scenes from Kunqu classics, such as The Peony Pavilion and The Palace of Eternal Youth will be analyzed and discussed before they are staged for appreciation. Under the teachers’ guidance, students will be able to experience the unity of song and dance as well as the artistic expression of emotions in the world of Kunqu opera.

title: Intercultural Communication and Engagement Abroad
components:
Discussion
Field Studies/Field-trip
Web-enhanced Teaching
Workshop
requirements: UGED2184 is double-coded with ENGE2180.Not for English; ELED majors; students taken ENGE2180.Open to students undergoing exchange.Co-requisite:UGFH1000,UGFN1000 etc (only applicable to students admitted to 4-year curriculum)
description: (UGED2184 is double-coded with ENGE2180.) This online course is designed to help students make the most of education abroad by enhancing their intercultural awareness and sensitivity as they explore the host environment and interact with locals and other international students. Except for a few pre-departure tasks, all work is done online while students are abroad. Through exposure to relevant theories, readings, and other resources, this course aims to help students develop a deeper understanding of what it means to be interculturally competent and global-minded as they immerse themselves in the host culture. While they critically reflect on their second language/intercultural interactions and share their experiences with peers, they are encouraged to become more curious, open-minded, and actively engaged in the world around them.

title: Literature and Human Rights
requirements: UGED2185 is double-coded with ENGE2120.Not for English; English Studies and English Language Education Majors; students who have taken ENGE2120.Co-requisite: UGFH1000, UGFN1000 or UGFN1001 (only applicable to students admitted to the 4-year curriculum)
description: (UGED2185 is double-coded with ENGE2120.) This course takes a closer look at the intimate connections between literature and human rights. The history of human rights has always been accompanied by literary texts; conversely, some of the most important literary texts in the world have focused on human rights issues. People who have suffered abuse and human rights violations have often articulated their painful stories in a variety of literary genres — in the hope of being heard, achieving recognition, bearing witness to events that have defined their lives. These stories thus constitute important documents around which rights campaigns and communities are built. During the course, we will look at the history of human rights literature, as well as various case studies — including Stolen Generation narratives in Australia, narratives by women who were forced into sexual slavery by the Japanese Imperial Army, political dissident narratives, and more recent refugee literature. No previous studies in literature needed to take this course. Students interested exploring the relevance of literary imagination and narrative for human rights discourse are welcome to attend this course.

title: American Popular Song Lyrics
requirements:
UGED2193 is double-coded with ENGE2160. 
Not for English; English Studies and English Language Education (ELED) Majors; and students who have taken ENGE2160. 
Co-requisite: Any course with “UGFH” or “UGFN” as prefix
description: (UGED2193 is double-coded with ENGE2160.) Focusing on song writers and performers from the USA, this course introduces students to the art of popular song lyrics of the twentieth century. In the process of studying American popular song lyrics, students will learn about such musical genres as “the blues,” “gospel,” “tin pan alley,” “folk,” “country,” and “rock and roll” as well as the elements of American history that give rise to each of these types of musical lyrics. Since one of the course elements is the relationship of musical lyrics to musical sound, we will spend considerable class time listening to popular songs , paying attention to the way a lyric’s meaning is conveyed through such elements as vocal style and musical arrangement.

title: Appreciation and Practice of Environmental Writing
requirements:
UGED2196 is double-coded with ENGE2520. 
Not for English; English Studies and English Language Education (ELED) Majors; and students who have taken ENGE2520. 
Co-requisite: Any course with “UGFH” or “UGFN” as prefix
description: (UGED2196 is double-coded with ENGE2520.) This course takes as its premise that environmental writing is environmental action. Environmental writing is also political engagement (biopolitics, as it were) as the ultimate aim of environmental writing is to effect policy change to protect, nurture, and sustain the environment and humankind. In this course, we will explore how to use different modes and genres of writing to effect environmental change. We will first examine the major elements of environmental writing through the exploration of different modes and genres, including children’s books, blogs, essays, poetry, songs, social media, Apps, newspaper articles, and posters. We will then examine the major environmental issues we are facing globally and in Hong Kong, and examine how environmental writing is currently being used in Hong Kong to engage the public and effect change. We will also investigate public awareness of the major environmental issues facing Hong Kong, to develop an understanding of how we can engage the public more effectively through writing. Finally, we will engage in our own environmental writing by creating three pieces of environmental writing, each examining the same environmental issue through a different type of writing. Key questions this course explores:• How can we use writing to raise awareness of environmental issues and effect environmental change?• What are the most pressing local and global environmental issues we face today? How is environmental writing currently being used in Hong Kong to engage the public and the government to respond to these issues? How can we use writing more effectively to engage the public and effect environmental change?

title: Psychology of Theatre
requirements:
Not for Psychology Majors.
Co-requisite: UGFH1000, UGFN1000 or UGFN1001 (only applicable to students admitted to the 4-year curriculum)
description: Psychology and theatre are integral parts of each other. Theatre explicates the psychology of human thinking and behaviors on stage and psychology processes underlie how artists enact their performance and how audience receives these performances. This is a general education course that introduces fundamental psychology concepts in the context of theatre. Students will learn emotions, cognitions and social processes of psychology and how they are integrated in the making of and experience of theatre. This course enables students to appreciate and analyze theatre from a psychological perspective. More importantly, this course allows students to understand oneself through psychology and theatre.While the title of the course is “Psychology of Theatre”, “theatre” is broadly defined to go beyond drama to cover related performing arts like dance, music, opera and alike. All these art forms share common elements of using the human body as an expression of thoughts and emotions via text, songs, movements and/or instruments in the theatre. The focus and majority of the illustrations are still about theatre as in drama. Coverage including related art forms is intentional because the same psychological elements are applicable to these different art forms. For example, the function of theatre as emotional expression applies to music, opera, dance and drama. Stage fright affects actors/actresses and also musicians and opera singers. The use of body as non-verbal expressions is essential to drama and dance. Psychosocial and interpersonal conflicts as depicted in stories are common to both drama and opera.

title: Seeing the World through Maps
requirements:
Not for Geography and Resource Management; and Urban Studies Majors.
Co-requisite: Any course with “UGFH” or “UGFN” as prefix
description: Maps are not just for "doing geography". People use maps in many disciplines, in their daily lives, in finding their way about town, in planning and in decision making. As a platform for displaying spatial information, maps have been used to depict and reveal spatial distribution and association and dynamic changes of various natural and social phenomena. Systematic analysis of laws, comprehensive evaluation, accurate forecast, rational planning, and efficient management can be achieved by using maps. This course introduces students the fundamental knowledge of maps, including the origin and development of maps, the social benefits and historical effects of maps, basic theory and technique of map use, different maps and their functions, and diversified applications of maps in the fields of national defense, economy, transportation, emergency response, public health, global change, etc. Modern cartographic technologies, such as computer cartography, remote sensing, geographic information system, and virtual graphical environment are also covered. Upon completion of this course, students are expected to appreciate the history and evolution of maps and their associated socio-economic and cultural contexts, to understand and apply basic concepts and skills in map use, to present data in the form of maps and to extract useful information from maps using the skills learned in class.

title: Insightful Decisions
requirements: Co-requisite: UGFH1000, UGFN1000 or UGFN1001 (only applicable to students admitted to the 4-year curriculum)
description: The University of Hong Kong (HKU), The Chinese University of Hong Kong (CUHK), The Hong Kong University of Science and Technology (HKUST), and The Hong Kong Polytechnic University (PolyU) are partners in a joint project entitled “The Responsive Universities: Appreciating Content Sharing in General Education”, which is funded by the UGC Funding Scheme for Teaching and Learning Related Proposals in the 2016-19 Triennium. Arising from this joint project, the four universities enter into an Agreement for Collaboration in Cross-institutional General Education Course Enrolment, under which students in the four universities can enrol in a list of designated General Education courses respectively offered by the four universities. This course, offered by The Hong Kong University of Science and Technology, is one of the designated courses under the Agreement.By confirming your enrolment of the course, you agree to give consent to CUHK in sharing your personal data among the partner institution of the Agreement for Collaboration in Cross-institutional Course Enrolment among HKU, CUHK, HKUST and PolyU, and to the partner institution for releasing your grades or other information relating to your study of the course to CUHK.The course helps students develop better analytical and decision making skills in approaching practical and important social and business issues. Students will derive solutions or conclusions that require critical thinking, creativity, quantitative analysis, and common sense. Cover topics in decision traps, quantitative decision models, statistical reasoning, computer tools, data-analysis techniques, etc. and, more importantly, how these decision analysis concepts and tools can be applied in a broad set of social and business problems.

title: Appreciation of Classical Poetry and Lyrics
requirements:
Not for Chinese Language and Literature; and Chinese Language Studies and Chinese Language Education (CLED) Majors.
Co-requisite: Any course with “UGFH” or “UGFN” as prefix
description: By analyzing selected classical poems and lyrics, this course introduces students to the styles of Chinese classical poetry as well as the value of Chinese poetry in modern society.

title: The Appreciation of Chinese Opera
requirements:
Not for Music Majors; and students who have taken GESC2400.
Co-requisite: Any course with “UGFH” or “UGFN” as prefix
description: This course makes extensive use of audio-visual materials, such as video documentary, audio tapes and slides, to introduce the basic concepts that are essential to the appreciation of Chinese opera. The following areas will be covered in the lectures and discussions: 1) the aesthetics of Chinese music and opera; 2) the understanding of Chinese opera in the context of Chinese culture; 3) the use of spatial and time elements in the performance of Chinese opera; 4) the fundamental music theories of Chinese opera; and 5) the stylistic characteristics of some of the representative regional styles of Chinese opera (Cantonese Opera, Peking Opera, Kunqu, etc.).

title: Journey into Madness: Conceptions of Mental Health and Mental Illness
components:
Field Studies/Field-trip
Independent Study
Lecture
Interactive Tutorial
Workshop
requirements:
Not for Psychology; Social Work Majors; and students who have taken SOWK2150 or UGED2611. 
Co-requisite: UGFH1000, UGFN1000 or UGFN1001 (only applicable to students admitted to the 4-year curriculum)
description: The University of Hong Kong (HKU), The Chinese University of Hong Kong (CUHK), The Hong Kong University of Science and Technology (HKUST), and The Hong Kong Polytechnic University (PolyU) are partners in a joint project entitled “The Responsive Universities: Appreciating Content Sharing in General Education”, which is funded by the UGC Funding Scheme for Teaching and Learning Related Proposals in the 2016-19 Triennium. Arising from this joint project, the four universities enter into an Agreement for Collaboration in Cross-institutional General Education Course Enrolment, under which students in the four universities can enrol in a list of designated General Education courses respectively offered by the four universities. This course, offered by The University of Hong Kong, is one of the designated courses under the Agreement.By confirming your enrolment of the course, you agree to give consent to CUHK in sharing your personal data among the partner institution of the Agreement for Collaboration in Cross-institutional Course Enrolment among HKU, CUHK, HKUST and PolyU, and to the partner institution for releasing your grades or other information relating to your study of the course to CUHK.Portrayed by mass media, there is an exaggerated link between mental illness and violence. Mental illness is often considered as an adversary that should be dealt with by medical professionals. Challenging this monopolized medical discourse on mental illness, this course aims to expand the students’ view to appreciate how mental illness has been psychologically influenced, socially constructed and policed, as well as culturally shaped. Coupling biochemistry’s knowledge of mental illness with self-reflections, students are expected to develop a critical and comprehensive understanding of mental illness and mental health. With the use of experiential exercises, case studies, and film viewing, students will be further encouraged to scrutinize mental health issues in their daily lives. As there is a growing number of individuals challenged by mental illnesses both locally and internationally, students will have high chance of encountering an individual with mental illnesses in their social circles, workplaces or even family in the future. The development of a comprehensive and critical view towards mental illnesses will definitely prepare them to face this future challenge.[All students will be required to plan and organize a compulsory experiential learning activity for service users at a mental health agency/setting during Reading Week. The experiential activity is compulsory and if interested students foresee that they cannot commit to this, they should not be enrolling in this course.]

title: Mental Health as a Public Health Issue
requirements:
UGED4926 is double-coded with CHPR4012. 
Not for CHPR and PHPC Majors; and students who have taken CHPR4012. 
Co-requisite: Any course with “UGFH” or “UGFN” as prefix (only applicable to students admitted to the 4-year curriculum)
description: (UGED4926 is double-coded with CHPR4012.) The course aims to enhance students’ knowledge on mental health and its determinants in public health and psychological perspectives. Major components of the course include 1) the epidemiology of mental health problems;  2) relationships among sociocultural factors, interpersonal resources, individual characteristics, and mental health; 3) mental health issues after adverse life events; 4) concepts and theories related to mental health promotion in the community; and 5) community health services and interventions to improve mental health.
